newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Reliance results surprise, tax move cited.
newsitem.headline: India's Reliance results surprise, tax move cited.

text.p: Reliance Industries Ltd surprised markets on Friday with a three percent rise in six-month net profit, but some analysts said an absence of a tax provision could explain the rise.
The market had been expecting a 25 to 30 percent fall in profits at the country's largest private firm.

Reliance's share price fell 0.50 paise on the Bombay Stock Exchange immediately after the petrochemicals and textiles firm's results, but recovered to close two rupees higher at 196.75. On the National Stock Exchange, the share rose 0.90 paise to 194.95 rupees in late afternoon trade.
"Everybody is actually baffled," said Jal Irani, analyst at Jardine Fleming Broking India.
"In a year when product prices dropped and costs increased on all fronts, this result is baffling," said another Bombay broker.
Stock markets were less startled by the 2.8 percent rise in Reliance's net profit to 6.51 billion rupees for April-September 1996 from 6.33 billion rupees in the first half of 1995/96.
The Bombay 30-share index rose 0.58 percent on the day but brokers said this was due marginally if at all to the Reliance result.
The company said operating profit rose to 8.94 billion rupees from 8.92 billion a year earlier.
It said sales rose to 40.41 billion rupees from 39.66 billion.
But Reliance did not provide for a 12.9 percent minimum tax imposed in India's July federal budget, which the company would be paying for the first time.

"In view of the substantial ongoing capital expenditure programme, the company has been advised that its income tax liability will be determinable only at the year-end," a Reliance statement said. "Therefore, provision for taxation, as applicable, will be made at the end of the year."

"We'll know more after the trip," said an equity analyst, referring to an analysts' meeting organised by Reliance on Saturday at Hazira on the western coast, the site of the firm's new petrochemical plant.
Analysts had estimated a tax burden of 1.5 billion rupees for the full year.
"Profits would have been some 12 percent lower if they had taken tax into account," said Vidyadhar Ginde, an analyst at Classic Share & Stock Broking Services in Bombay.

He said high capital costs of new projects and depreciation would continue to burden Reliance in the second half of 1996/97, but there were signs that petrochemical prices, which fell steeply during the period under review, were looking up.

Reliance said polyester prices were improving. "The international price of PSF (polyester staple fibre) has recently increased from a low of 95 cents per kg to about $1.10, a rise of 15 percent," a company release said.
